rubric.name: CC Audience Awareness
rubric.description: Every CC'd person is there for a reason, and the email is crafted knowing they will read it. The primary recipient gets the ask; the CC'd audience gets a deliberate signal — accountability, visibility, or alignment.

rubric.name: Directive Clarity
rubric.description: Non-negotiable requests use direct language, never conditional framing. 'Please submit by Friday' not 'Would you be able to submit by Friday?' Conditional language is reserved exclusively for genuinely optional items.

dimensions.label: Required actions do not use 'if possible', 'would you be able to', or 'it would be great if'
Truly optional items use optionality language to distinguish them from requirements
The level of directness matches the sender's authority relative to the recipient

rubric.name: Recipient-Interest Framing
rubric.description: Requests are positioned as serving the recipient's interest, even when the ask primarily benefits the sender. The reframe must be genuine — not a transparent manipulation.

dimensions.label: The email explains how the ask serves the recipient or their team, not just the sender
The benefit framing is credible — the recipient would agree it serves them if asked

That's not what I care about. What I care about is that the CC list as a whole sends a deliberate organizational signal, and that nothing leaks to the wrong audience. In Round 2, the grader actually docked points because the Board Chair's 'specific signal is entirely unaddressed' — but the Board Chair's signal IS the CC itself. Their presence on the email tells the department heads this has board-level visibility. That's intentional and sufficient. The grader is confusing 'deliberate signal' with 'explicit verbal acknowledgment of each person's role.'

Penalizing an email because the Board Chair isn't given a named functional role in the body text
Treating the CC list as only meaningful if the email verbally unpacks each person's presence

Subject: Hiring Freeze Effective Immediately — Action Required from All Department Heads

---

To: Department Heads
CC: [CFO Name], [Board Chair Name]

---

Team,

Effective today, we are pausing all open requisitions and halting new hiring activity across the company. This applies to every department, without exception.

I want to be direct with you about why.

The market has shifted faster than our original projections accounted for, and protecting the financial health of the company right now means making hard calls before we're forced to make harder ones. A hiring freeze is the right lever to pull — it preserves runway, keeps the people we have employed, and buys us the time to make thoughtful decisions rather than reactive ones. This is not a sign that the business is broken. It is a sign that we are managing it carefully.

Here is what I need from each of you:

- **Audit your open roles** and flag any that you consider operationally critical. Submit that list to [CFO Name] by end of day Friday.
- **Pause all active searches** immediately, including roles in late-stage interviews. Candidates in final stages should be notified with care — I'll leave the language to your judgment, but treat people well.
- **Do not communicate this externally** beyond active candidates until we release internal guidance, which will go out by [date].

I recognize this creates real pressure on teams that were already stretched. That's not lost on me. If a role represents a genuine operational risk to pause, the process above gives you a path to escalate it — use it.

[CFO Name] and [Board Chair Name] are copied here and are aligned on this direction.

We'll talk through the broader context and your questions on [date/time of all-hands or leadership call].

[CEO Name]

Subject: Hiring Freeze Effective Immediately — Action Required from All Department Heads

---

To: Department Heads
CC: [CFO Name], [Board Chair Name]

---

Team,

Effective today, all open requisitions are paused and no new hiring activity moves forward — across every department, no exceptions.

I want to give you the honest version, not the polished one.

We are in a period where the cost of moving too slowly is lower than the cost of moving too fast. Our projections shifted, and the responsible move is to create breathing room now rather than face a much harder conversation six months from now. The people sitting in your organizations today keep their jobs because we make this call today. That tradeoff is worth it.

I also know what this means for you personally. You made commitments to your teams about growth. You have searches underway that you've invested months in. You may have a candidate who accepted an offer in good faith. None of that is invisible to me, and it's exactly why this email comes from me directly — not from HR, not from Finance.

Here is what this looks like in practice:

- **Audit your open roles** and identify anything you consider a genuine operational risk to pause. Get that list to [CFO Name] by end of day Friday — that process exists so your judgment gets heard, and I want you to use it seriously.
- **Pause all active searches now**, including roles in late-stage interviews. For candidates in final stages, handle those conversations with the care you'd want if the situation were reversed.
- **Hold external communication** until we release coordinated messaging, which goes out no later than [date].

The escalation path on critical roles isn't a formality — it's how your operational reality shapes what comes next. If a pause creates a genuine risk for your team, flag it.

[CFO Name] and [Board Chair Name] are copied on this note. This decision has full organizational alignment behind it, and they are here as a reflection of that.

We'll talk through this together on [date/time]. Bring your questions.

[CEO Name]

rubric_snapshot.user_goals_summary: Writes emails that navigate organizational power dynamics with precision. Every word is chosen for how it lands with the primary recipient AND the CC'd audience. Treats email as a tool of organizational choreography, not just communication.

rubric.name: CC Audience Awareness
rubric.description: Every CC'd person is there for a reason, and the email is crafted knowing they will read it. The primary recipient gets the ask; the CC'd audience gets a deliberate signal — accountability, visibility, or alignment.

dimensions.label: Each CC'd person receives a specific signal from the email (accountability, awareness, endorsement)
Nothing in the email reveals information inappropriate for any CC'd reader
The primary recipient and their specific ask are unambiguous despite the CC'd audience
The CC list itself sends a message — the choice of who is included is deliberate

rubric.name: Directive Clarity
rubric.description: Non-negotiable requests use direct language, never conditional framing. 'Please submit by Friday' not 'Would you be able to submit by Friday?' Conditional language is reserved exclusively for genuinely optional items.

dimensions.label: Required actions do not use 'if possible', 'would you be able to', or 'it would be great if'
Truly optional items use optionality language to distinguish them from requirements
The level of directness matches the sender's authority relative to the recipient

rubric.name: Recipient-Interest Framing
rubric.description: Requests are positioned as serving the recipient's interest, even when the ask primarily benefits the sender. The reframe must be genuine — not a transparent manipulation.

dimensions.label: The email explains how the ask serves the recipient or their team, not just the sender
The benefit framing is credible — the recipient would agree it serves them if asked
Avoids 'we need this for our planning' when 'this helps your team plan' is more accurate

rubric.name: Voice Matching
rubric.description: When writing on behalf of an executive, the email sounds like that person — mirroring their vocabulary, sentence length, and communication style — not like a generic professional email.

dimensions.label: Uses words and phrases the named executive would actually use
Sentence length, formality level, and directness match the executive's established pattern
The email could not be attributed to 'any senior leader' — it has a specific voice

rubric_snapshot.coaching_notes: Carmen treats every email as having two audiences — the TO and the CC — and writes for both simultaneously. Non-negotiable: conditional language is never used for non-negotiable requests. Will reject drafts that sound generically polished rather than like the specific executive's voice.

Subject: Hiring Freeze Effective Immediately — Action Required from All Department Heads

---

To: Department Heads
CC: [CFO Name], [Board Chair Name]

---

Team,

Effective today, all open requisitions are paused. No new hiring moves forward — any department, no exceptions.

Here's what I want you to know before you read the bullet points.

We are in a period where acting early is the only responsible option. Our projections shifted, and the gap between where we planned to be and where we are is real. A hiring freeze now means the people already in your organizations keep their jobs. That is the tradeoff, and it's the right one.

I also know what lands on your desk when you read this. Commitments you made to your teams about headcount. Searches you've run for months. Possibly a candidate who said yes. I'm not asking you to pretend those costs don't exist — I'm asking you to absorb them with me, and to trust that this is the version of hard that keeps us from a harder version later.

This email comes from me directly — not from HR, not through a policy update — because you deserve to hear it that way. [CFO Name] and [Board Chair Name] are copied here: [CFO Name] because the financial framework behind this decision runs through their office, and [Board Chair Name] because this has full board visibility. You should know who is in the room.

What I need from you:

- **Audit your open roles** and identify anything you consider operationally critical to keep moving. Submit that list to [CFO Name] by end of day Friday. That process is real — your judgment on what your team cannot absorb is exactly the input that shapes what exceptions, if any, get made.
- **Pause all active searches immediately**, including roles in late-stage interviews. For candidates in final rounds, handle those conversations the way you'd want to be handled. I'll leave the specifics to you.
- **Hold all external communication** on this until coordinated messaging goes out — no later than [date].

The escalation path on critical roles isn't a courtesy. It's how your operational reality gets factored into what comes next. If a pause creates a genuine risk for your team, flag it.

We'll talk through this on [date/time]. Bring your questions — I mean that.

[CEO Name]

---

To: Department Heads
CC: [CFO Name], [Board Chair Name]

---

Team,

Effective today, all open requisitions are paused. No new hiring moves forward — any department, no exceptions.

Here's what I want you to know before you get to the action items.

Our projections shifted, and the gap between where we planned to be and where we are is real enough that acting now is the only responsible move. A freeze today means the people already sitting in your organizations keep their jobs. That's the tradeoff I'm making, and I'd make it again.

I know what this drops on your desk. Headcount commitments you made to your teams. Searches you've run for months. Maybe a candidate who already said yes. I'm not asking you to pretend those costs aren't real — I'm asking you to carry them with me, and to trust that this version of hard is what keeps us from a harder one later.

This comes from me directly — not through HR, not buried in a policy update — because you deserve to hear it that way.

[CFO Name] is copied because the financial architecture behind this decision runs through their office — they are the right person to receive your escalations and the right person to hold the line on exceptions. [Board Chair Name] is copied because this decision carries full board visibility; their presence here is not incidental. You should know exactly who is in the room and why.

What I need from you:

- **Audit your open roles** and identify anything you consider operationally critical to keep moving. Get that list to [CFO Name] by end of day Friday. This isn't a formality — your read on what your team cannot absorb is the input that determines whether exceptions get made.
- **Pause all active searches now**, including roles in late-stage interviews. For candidates in final rounds, handle those conversations the way you'd want to be handled. I'll leave the how to you.
- **Hold all external communication** until coordinated messaging goes out — no later than [date].

If a pause creates a genuine operational risk for your team, the escalation path above is how that gets surfaced. Use it.

We'll talk through this on [date/time]. Bring your questions — I mean that.

[CEO Name]

[CEO Name]

rubric_snapshot.user_goals_summary: Writes emails that navigate organizational power dynamics with precision. Every word is chosen for how it lands with the primary recipient AND the CC'd audience. Treats email as a tool of organizational choreography, not just communication.

rubric.name: CC Audience Awareness
rubric.description: Every CC'd person is there for a reason, and the email is crafted knowing they will read it. The primary recipient gets the ask; the CC'd audience gets a deliberate signal — accountability, visibility, or alignment.

dimensions.label: Each CC'd person receives a specific signal from the email (accountability, awareness, endorsement)
Nothing in the email reveals information inappropriate for any CC'd reader
The primary recipient and their specific ask are unambiguous despite the CC'd audience
The CC list itself sends a message — the choice of who is included is deliberate

negative_examples: Requiring a separate sentence addressed to each CC'd person explaining why they're included
Penalizing an email because the Board Chair isn't given a named functional role in the body text
Treating the CC list as only meaningful if the email verbally unpacks each person's presence
rubric.clarification: The CC list itself is a signal — who is included, at what level, sends a message to the primary recipient about authority, alignment, and visibility. The email body should acknowledge the CC'd audience exists (so the primary recipient knows they're being watched), but it does NOT need to individually address or explain each CC'd person's role. The key tests are: (1) does the primary recipient understand the stakes implied by who's watching, (2) does nothing in the email reveal information inappropriate for any CC'd reader, and (3) was the choice of who to include deliberate. Round 2 should not have been scored lower than Round 1 on this criterion.

rubric.name: Directive Clarity
rubric.description: Non-negotiable requests use direct language, never conditional framing. 'Please submit by Friday' not 'Would you be able to submit by Friday?' Conditional language is reserved exclusively for genuinely optional items.

dimensions.label: Required actions do not use 'if possible', 'would you be able to', or 'it would be great if'
Truly optional items use optionality language to distinguish them from requirements
The level of directness matches the sender's authority relative to the recipient

rubric.name: Recipient-Interest Framing
rubric.description: Requests are positioned as serving the recipient's interest, even when the ask primarily benefits the sender. The reframe must be genuine — not a transparent manipulation.

dimensions.label: The email explains how the ask serves the recipient or their team, not just the sender
The benefit framing is credible — the recipient would agree it serves them if asked
Avoids 'we need this for our planning' when 'this helps your team plan' is more accurate

negative_examples: Requiring recipient-benefit language to appear before org-level rationale
Treating any sentence that mentions the sender's or org's needs as a violation of this criterion
Scoring based on where in the email the recipient framing appears rather than whether it's genuine and credible
rubric.clarification: Recipient-interest framing means the overall ask is positioned as serving the recipient — it does NOT mean every sentence must center the recipient, and it does NOT mean org-level context is forbidden. The test is: would the recipient, reading this email, feel that their reality was seen and that the ask was framed with their interests in mind? Round 2 does this better than Round 1 because it explicitly names the personal costs to department heads and frames the escalation path as 'your judgment gets heard.' That's genuine, not manipulative. Round 2 deserves a higher score on this criterion than Round 1, not the same or lower.

rubric.name: Voice Matching
rubric.description: When writing on behalf of an executive, the email sounds like that person — mirroring their vocabulary, sentence length, and communication style — not like a generic professional email.

dimensions.label: Uses words and phrases the named executive would actually use
Sentence length, formality level, and directness match the executive's established pattern
The email could not be attributed to 'any senior leader' — it has a specific voice

negative_examples: Scoring a draft low purely because no prior email samples from the executive were provided in the prompt
Treating 'could plausibly be attributed to many senior leaders who favor this style' as a failing when the style is at least specific and consistent
Ignoring that Round 2's 'honest version, not the polished one' framing is a deliberate voice choice that distinguishes it from generic executive communication
rubric.clarification: Voice matching should be evaluated on a spectrum. When prior voice data exists, the draft must mirror that specific person's known patterns — that's the highest bar. When no prior data exists, the criterion evaluates whether the draft (a) avoids generic professional polish, (b) constructs a consistent and specific voice that could be attributed to a particular type of leader, and (c) would not be mistaken for a template. Round 2 clears that bar meaningfully better than Round 1 and should score higher, not lower. The grader has it backwards — Round 2's candid, self-aware, slightly unguarded tone is exactly the kind of specificity this criterion rewards.
